prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The counter occupies the lower foreground about 0.3–0.8 m from the camera wearer, while the register and nearby containers rise roughly 0.6–1.0 m away; the standing person is behind them at about 1–1.5 m, partly occluded below the torso by the counter. The paper bag remains beyond and left of the register, about 0.8–1.2 m from the camera and within roughly half a metre of the person, while background shelves and displays are several metres farther away. Across the five frames, the register and person become larger and shift from right toward the centre before the person moves toward the right edge, consistent mainly with the camera approaching and turning right rather than a clear retreat by the person. The depth map makes foreground-to-background ordering and counter occlusion clearer than RGB, but its absolute metric distances are only rough, and object edges, the person's arms, reflective surfaces, and the over-bright lower foreground appear unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The map separates the person behind the counter from the keyboard/register-sized object in the foreground and intermittently isolates smaller items such as a bottle and objects labelled book or TV. It shows the person mostly facing the camera wearer, with the torso roughly 1–1.5 m ahead and the foreground counter objects within about 0.3–0.8 m of the wearer; the person's extended hand is within arm's reach of both the counter surface and nearby objects. Over time, the person mask grows and shifts toward the right edge, while the large foreground-object masks slide across the lower frame as the camera moves closer and turns right; parts of the person, counter, and objects remain cropped or mutually occluded. The masks clarify object boundaries that blend together in RGB, but labels and instances are inconsistent—especially the large regions called keyboard or book—and several small objects disappear, merge, or receive incomplete masks between frames.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects only magenta hand landmarks: a hand appears near the upper middle in frame 2, near the centre in frame 3, right of centre in frame 4, and near the upper-right in frame 5, while frame 1 has no reliable skeleton. These landmarks place the visible hand about 1–1.5 m from the camera wearer and above the counter, within the standing person's arm's reach; its changing image position follows the camera's rightward turn and changing proximity. The finger geometry gives clearer hand orientation than RGB in some frames, but no yellow body skeleton is visible, so torso direction, gaze direction, inter-person distances, and whether anyone looks at the camera cannot be established reliably from this map alone. The hand skeletons are also incomplete and sometimes oddly bent or detached from the visible arm, especially where the hand is small, cropped, or occluded.
